title: Kevin O’Leary says he still owns Bitcoin, but two risks have his attention
detail:
Kevin O’Leary says he still owns Bitcoin, but two risks have his attention
Bibhu Pattnaik
Wed, October 28, 2026 at 4:15 PM EDT 2 min read
BTC-USD
IBM
Trade BTC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Kevin O'Leary says he has not walked away from Bitcoin, even as the asset struggles to push higher.

In a post on X, the Shark Tank investor named two factors behind the plateau and said he is tracking both closely.

Why Bitcoin is stuck

"Why is Bitcoin plateauing?" O'Leary asked. His answer: institutions want regulatory clarity before they invest, and quantum computing has become a growing concern for some investors.

"Why is Bitcoin plateauing? Two factors are weighing on it: institutions want regulatory clarity before they invest, and quantum computing has become a growing concern for some investors," he wrote in his post.

"I still own Bitcoin, but I'm paying close attention to both sides of this shift," he added.

He also sees opportunity in the second risk. "The quantum opportunity is also why I'm looking at companies like IBM," O'Leary said, suggesting the same technology that worries Bitcoin holders could reward investors elsewhere.

Yesterday angel investor Jason Calacanis had issued one of his bluntest warnings on Bitcoin, telling followers to sell and move their money.

Related: Elon Musk has a bold answer to America's $40 trillion debt crisis

He predicted Bitcoin "will test the 57k low again in the next 12 months," pointing to outflows from Bitcoin exchange-traded funds as a warning sign.

What he said earlier

The post echoes comments O'Leary made last month. Speaking at the Avalanche Summit in New York, he said he was adding crypto positions again.

"I'm back in the saddle buying new positions, putting my bets on for this next cycle," he said. He added that he is waiting for a major stock exchange to adopt a blockchain, which he called a "watershed moment."

On regulation, O'Leary had said he expects crypto legislation to return after the CLARITY Act's Senate setback, since lawmakers are working on tax policy for digital assets. He does not expect a bill before the midterms.

On quantum, he had said in a separate interview that Bitcoin could reach $1 million, but only if the industry settles the doubt around the technology. He called the threat "Q-Day," the point at which quantum machines could break the algorithms and encryption protecting blockchains.

O'Leary has also said Bitcoin could eventually take a 1% to 3% share of alternative-asset allocation, similar to what institutions hold in gold.

title: Why Did D-Wave Quantum Stock Fall?

Why Did D-Wave Quantum Stock Fall?

Shares of D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) fell 65.4% in the twelve months to October 27, 2026, trailing the 13.6% return of the S&P 500 over the same period. The decline spanned a full year of earnings reports, beginning with the third-quarter 2025 results on November 6, 2025, and ending with the second-quarter 2026 release on August 6, 2026. So what changed in D-Wave's own business over that year?

D-Wave's Sales Turned Down In 2026

D-Wave finished 2025 with growing sales, reporting on February 26, 2026, that fourth-quarter 2025 revenue was up 19.2% from a year earlier. The first-quarter results on May 12, 2026, showed revenue down 80.9% from a year earlier, because the year-earlier quarter included an unusually large amount of sales. The company had generated about $15 million in that year-earlier quarter, bringing in more than the next three quarters of 2025 combined.

The decline did not deepen in the latest quarter. On the August 6 call, management said second-quarter revenue of $3.1 million was essentially flat with a year earlier.

D-Wave's slide was part of a broader drop in quantum computing stocks. In October, law firms filed a putative securities fraud class action against D-Wave on behalf of purchasers who acquired shares between February 26 and August 25, 2026, alleging that the company overstated its business and system delivery prospects. Over the same twelve months, Rigetti Computing lost 69% and IonQ lost 48%.

Selling Less, D-Wave Is Also Losing More

D-Wave generated $12.4 million in revenue over the twelve months to June 2026, down from $22.3 million in the twelve months before. The company's operating loss widened over the same period to $171 million, from $78.7 million. Management said its adjusted EBITDA loss in the second quarter grew mainly because of staff costs for faster product development and sales.

Selling whole systems generated most of D-Wave's revenue in fiscal 2025, accounting for $16.2 million of its $24.6 million in revenue. Management expects the fourth quarter of 2026 to bring in the majority of its 2026 revenue, because that is when it expects its systems to ship.

Even after the stock decline, D-Wave's market value is 362 times its sales over the last twelve months, compared with 3.2 times for the S&P 500. This price appears to assume that D-Wave will sell many times what it sells today.

What D-Wave Still Has: Cash And Contracts

Despite the share price fall, D-Wave is not short of cash. The company held $546 million in cash and short-term investments at June 30, 2026, against $48.1 million of debt. Its cash was more than four times the $120 million of free cash flow D-Wave used over the twelve months to June.

title: IBM Stock or Bitcoin? Quantum is Making Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary Rethink
detail:
IBM Stock or Bitcoin? Quantum is Making Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary Rethink
Phil Haunhorst
Wed, October 28, 2026 at 9:12 AM EDT 2 min read
BTC-USD
IBM
Trade BTC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by BeInCrypto

Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary says he is looking at IBM as quantum computing fears weigh on Bitcoin (BTC). He also says institutions want regulatory clarity before they buy, keeping the asset flat.

Still, O'Leary says he holds on to his Bitcoin. His IBM interest suggests part of the quantum trade could flow toward tech stocks instead of crypto.

Why Are Institutions Still Waiting on Washington?

On the regulatory side, Washington has yet to deliver. The stalled CLARITY Act would set federal rules for crypto markets.

However, the bill has not moved since a 49 to 50 Senate vote in September fell short of the 60 votes needed.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin still trades well below its October 2025 record high.

Bitcoin Price Performance. Source: BeInCrypto

The concern is not new for O'Leary. In September, he made quantum fears the core of his $1 million condition for Bitcoin.

Does O'Leary Overstate the Quantum Threat to Bitcoin?

O'Leary is not the only big name raising the alarm. TRON founder Justin Sun recently turned bearish on Bitcoin over quantum and artificial intelligence (AI) risks.

Others see more time. Casa security chief Jameson Lopp says a quantum computer able to break Bitcoin remains orders of magnitude away.

The hardware gap supports that view. Google's Willow chip has 105 qubits, while Google puts the count needed to break Bitcoin at under 500,000.

Venture capitalist Tim Draper goes further, arguing that quantum computers would crack banks before Bitcoin.

O'Leary did not detail his IBM thesis. However, the company has already put dates on its quantum push.

In July, IBM CEO Arvind Krishna said quantum computing should measurably affect IBM's revenue by 2028 or 2029.

IBM also plans to launch Starling, which it calls the first large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer, by 2029. Such machines can correct their own errors, a key step before any real threat to Bitcoin's cryptography.

In effect, IBM gives O'Leary exposure to the same quantum progress he sees as a risk for Bitcoin.

IBM shares have recovered over the past month but still trade below their level a year ago.

International Business Machines (IBM) Stock Price. Source: TradingView

Until Bitcoin's quantum migration and the CLARITY Act both move forward, the two forces O'Leary named may keep large Bitcoin allocators cautious.

JPMorgan Chase, Advanced Micro Devices and Coca-Cola are among seven more companies keeping tokenized versions of their shares off the trading venue Intercontinental Exchange and OKX plan to run, a revised public notice the venue posted dated Oct. 27 shows. Its objection list now runs to 33 issuers, up from 26 in the version dated a day earlier.

The other four new names are Applied Materials, Adobe, Dell Technologies and Sandisk. All seven sit at the end of the list, after the 26 issuers carried over from the previous version, among them Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Oracle, IBM and Intel. JPMorgan joins Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo as the third bank on the list.

All seven were among the 63 tickers that the venue's first notice, dated Oct. 4, listed for tokenized trading. Like the earlier versions, the new notice gives no reason for any objection and no launch date.

Get Unchained's crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter.

How the List Grows

Under the SEC's exemption for tokenized stock venues, an order dated Sept. 17, a venue has to notify an issuer before it trades a token of that company's stock created by an unaffiliated third party. A timely written objection from the issuer, sent within 30 calendar days of receiving that notice, keeps the token off the venue, and the venue then has five business days to disclose the objection in an amended public notice.

The tally has risen with each revision: nine on Oct. 15, when five, including Broadcom and Verizon, opted out, then 16 on Oct. 19 and 22 on Oct. 23, when six, including Wells Fargo, Arm and Intuit, were added.

Hosting Changes

Alibaba Cloud (Singapore) no longer appears in the table's technology and hosting rows. Amazon Web Services, already listed as storing participants' personal data, is now also named as the cloud services provider for the venue's website, back-end systems and databases. OKX Inc. now appears next to OKX Technology Inc. as a developer of the venue's software. A separate passage on disaster recovery still says those off-chain systems are hosted by Alibaba Cloud.

The notice keeps the risk disclosures from earlier versions, including that smart contract changes "take effect without a timelock, so TSV Participants may receive no advance notice of an upgrade."

Seagate Technology Holdings plc STX reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 non-GAAP earnings of $7.68 per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $7.44 and exceeding the high end of management's guidance of $7.30 per share (+/- 20 cents). The bottom line also expanded a massive 194% year over year, driven by robust Data Center demand, favorable pricing and solid operational execution.

Non-GAAP revenues of $4.2 billion surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 3%. Revenues were above the midpoint of guidance, increasing 61% year over year. The uptrend highlights rising storage demand, disciplined pricing and advances in HAMR technology. STX expects strong sequential revenue growth and gross margin expansion throughout fiscal 2027, cushioned by robust demand visibility extending beyond 2030 and an areal density-driven technology roadmap designed to capitalize on this growth.

Its technology roadmap is projected to support mid-20% annualized nearline exabyte supply growth. Most nearline exabyte supply is secured under long-term agreements through 2028, with some cloud customer contracts extending to 2030.

Seagate Technology Holdings PLC Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise
Seagate Technology Holdings PLC Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Seagate Technology Holdings PLC price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Seagate Technology Holdings PLC Quote

STX expects HAMR to account for roughly 50% of nearline exabyte shipments by the end of 2026, with Mozaic 4 representing about half of HAMR shipments. Mozaic 4, offering up to 44TB, is ramping with two leading CSPs, while additional qualifications across global CSPs and enterprise OEMs are expected in the coming months. Furthermore, development of Mozaic 5, featuring capacities above 50TB, remains on track, with customer qualification shipments expected to begin in late 2027. Seagate also demonstrated 8TB per disk in the lab, reinforcing the potential of HAMR and its areal-density roadmap to drive future capacity growth.

STX's Revenues by End Market

The data center accounted for 81% of total revenue, at $3.4 billion, representing an 18% sequential increase and 63% year-over-year growth. Global cloud customers drove a lion's share of data center revenue and exabyte demand, a trend expected to persist as Mozaic 4 production ramps.

Enterprise OEM demand also strengthened, with revenue from these markets posting double-digit sequential and year-over-year growth for the sixth consecutive quarter, driven by rising demand for scalable, high-capacity storage amid growing AI inference and agent-based workloads.
